task_row_model.query: In Python using psycopg2, what is the safest way to build and execute a parameterized INSERT to avoid SQL injection and ensure correct handling of NULL values and inserting list/array data? Provide examples and note common pitfalls.

documents.content: SQL injection is an attack that occurs when untrusted input is interpolated directly into SQL statements. The recommended defense is to use parameterized queries: the SQL string contains placeholders and the driver sends data separately, so values are never treated as SQL. Most adapters use placeholders like %s and will escape or bind parameters for you. Understanding how placeholders differ from string formatting and avoiding building SQL with concatenation are essential. This explanation covers why parameterization works but does not show library-specific code or how to handle NULLs or array columns in PostgreSQL.

Connection pooling with psycopg2 can improve application performance by reusing database connections rather than opening a new TCP and authentication handshake for each request. The library provides ThreadedConnectionPool and SimpleConnectionPool; you create a pool at startup and call getconn()/putconn() per request. Pools should be sized according to expected concurrent work and database limits. Use context managers or try/finally to ensure connections return to the pool. This note focuses on pooling behavior, limits, and lifecycle management and does not cover statement parameterization or safe construction of SQL queries.

Use psycopg2 parameterized statements and helper utilities. For a simple INSERT, include %s placeholders and pass a tuple: cur.execute("INSERT INTO users (name, age, bio) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", (name, age, bio)) — to insert NULL pass Python None. For bulk inserts or lists of rows use psycopg2.extras.execute_values to efficiently insert many records: execute_values(cur, "INSERT INTO tags (item_id, tag) VALUES %s", data_list). For PostgreSQL array columns, psycopg2 adapts Python lists to SQL arrays when used as a parameter: cur.execute("INSERT INTO doc (id, keywords) VALUES (%s, %s)", (doc_id, ['a','b'])). Never build SQL by formatting strings for values; use sql.Identifier/sql.SQL for dynamic identifiers if needed.

ORMs like SQLAlchemy abstract parameterization and are a good alternative if you prefer high-level models. When using the Core layer or ORM, queries are composed with bind parameters automatically: stmt = users.insert().values(name=bindparam('name')) and execution with connection.execute(stmt, {'name': value}) ensures values are bound. ORMs also map Python None to SQL NULL. While SQLAlchemy manages many safety concerns, understanding raw SQL and the underlying driver behavior is important when using text() statements or executing raw SQL fragments that may require manual binding.

Backing up and restoring PostgreSQL databases is commonly done with pg_dump and pg_restore. Use pg_dump -Fc for a custom-format dump and pg_restore to selectively restore objects. For small databases, plain SQL dumps are convenient: pg_dump > backup.sql and psql to restore. Logical backups capture schema and data; physical backups use filesystem-level tools and require consistent base backups and WAL replay. This discussion covers choices for backup formats, compression, and restore strategies, and is unrelated to constructing parameterized queries within application code.
